wine.name: Côte-Rôtie La Mouline
wine.classification: A cru of the Rhône Valley, above Côtes du Rhône and its Villages
wine.grapes: Syrah, the great majority, with about a tenth of Viognier grown among the vines and fermented with it.
wine.sites: La Mouline, a lieu-dit on the Côte Blonde south of Ampuis: old vines on narrow stone terraces curved round the slope like an amphitheatre, on pale granite and gneiss.
wine.making: The Syrah and the Viognier are picked together and fermented together in vat. The wine then spends about 42 months in new oak barrels, three and a half years and far longer than the custom of the appellation, before it is bottled at Ampuis.
wine.glass: Violet, raspberry and blackberry over smoked bacon and black pepper, with a lift of apricot skin from the Viognier; silky and perfumed rather than heavy, the new oak folded in as vanilla and toast, on fine, ripe tannin.
wine.ageing: Open sooner than the house's La Landonne, it wants eight to ten years to absorb its oak, and a strong vintage keeps for decades.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour or two, an old one gently off its sediment; a large Burgundy glass for the perfume.

label.means: The roasted slope above Ampuis, the northernmost cru of the Rhône: Syrah with up to a fifth Viognier in the vat.
The lieu-dit on the Côte Blonde, first bottled on its own with the 1966 vintage.
The house of Ampuis that grows, makes and bottles the wine.

records.table: From one lieu-dit on the Côte Blonde, La Mouline is E. Guigal's Côte-Rôtie of Syrah fermented with about a tenth of Viognier, then raised 42 months in new oak. Violets and smoked bacon over silk, it wants a decanter and a large glass.
records.story: Côte-Rôtie was a small and struggling vineyard when the founder of this house, who had worked since boyhood in the cellars of the Ampuis merchant Vidal-Fleury, set up on his own in 1946. When he lost his sight in 1961, his son, then in his teens, took charge. The slope above the village was already told as a story: a lord of Maugiron, it is said, left one hillside to a fair daughter and one to a dark one, and the names Côte Blonde and Côte Brune stuck to rocks that truly differ. With the 1966 vintage the house bottled the old vines of La Mouline, on the Blonde, as a wine of their own, when Côte-Rôtie was almost always a blend of the whole slope. La Landonne followed in 1978 and La Turque in 1985, the trio the trade calls the La La wines, and in 1984 Guigal bought Vidal-Fleury, the house where its founder had begun. The three single vineyards carried the name of Côte-Rôtie far beyond the Rhône and helped bring abandoned terraces back into use. La Mouline remains the lesson in co-fermented Viognier: the white grape lends the perfume, the Syrah gives the frame.

others.name: Côte-Rôtie La Landonne
others.note: From the Côte Brune, Syrah alone, first made in 1978: the firmest and slowest of the three.

others.name: Côte-Rôtie La Turque
others.note: From the Côte Brune with a little Viognier, first made in 1985, the third of the La La wines.

others.name: Côte-Rôtie Château d'Ampuis
others.note: A blend of several lieux-dits, the step below the La La wines, named for the château in the village.

traps: La Mouline is on the Côte Blonde; La Landonne and La Turque are on the Côte Brune.
La Landonne is Syrah alone; La Mouline and La Turque are fermented with a little Viognier, which goes into the vat with the Syrah, never into the finished wine.
Vidal-Fleury has been Guigal's since 1984 yet keeps its own label, so a Vidal-Fleury Côte-Rôtie is not a Guigal wine.

cards.front: E. Guigal's La Mouline: which side of Côte-Rôtie, and what grows among its Syrah?
cards.back: The Côte Blonde; about a tenth of Viognier, picked and fermented with the Syrah.

cards.front: Guigal's three La La Côte-Rôties: their first vintages, in order?
cards.back: La Mouline 1966, La Landonne 1978, La Turque 1985.

questions.q: A guest finds apricot and violet in a glass of Guigal's La Mouline and asks where they come from. What do you say?
opts: Viognier fermented with the Syrah
Viognier blended in after fermenting
A late harvest of ripe Syrah
A share of Marsanne in the blend
questions.exp: La Mouline carries about a tenth of Viognier grown among its vines and fermented with the Syrah; Côte-Rôtie lets the white grape into the vat, never into the finished wine, and Marsanne is a grape of Hermitage.

questions.q: In 1984 E. Guigal bought the Ampuis merchant house where its founder had worked as a boy. Which house was it?
opts: Vidal-Fleury
Paul Jaboulet Aîné
Delas Frères
M. Chapoutier
questions.exp: The founder worked at Vidal-Fleury before he set up in 1946, and Guigal bought it in 1984 while keeping its label; Jaboulet and Chapoutier are houses of Tain-l'Hermitage.

wine.name: Hermitage La Chapelle
wine.classification: A cru of the Rhône Valley, above Côtes du Rhône and its Villages
wine.grapes: Syrah alone, though the appellation would allow a little Marsanne and Roussanne in the vat.
wine.sites: Chiefly Les Bessards, steep granite at the western end of the south facing hill, and Le Méal, warmer and stonier in its middle, with smaller parts from other climats.
wine.making: The climats are fermented in vat and blended into the one wine, which is raised in oak barrels, some of them new, for well over a year before it is bottled at the house in Tain.
wine.glass: Blackberry, black olive and smoked bacon over violet, iron and cracked pepper; dense and closed when young, with firm tannin, turning with age to leather, truffle and dried fig.
wine.ageing: Closed for ten to fifteen years after a strong vintage, it then opens slowly; its 1961 and 1978 have lasted for decades.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for two hours or more, an old one gently off its heavy sediment; a large Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The single hill above Tain and its appellation: red from Syrah, white from Marsanne and Roussanne.
The house's name for its red, after the chapel at the summit of the hill; no vineyard bears it.
The house; aîné means the elder, for the founder's elder son.

records.table: Named for the little chapel at the summit of the hill, Hermitage La Chapelle is Paul Jaboulet Aîné's red from the granite of Les Bessards and the terraces of Le Méal. All Syrah, black olive and smoked meat, it needs ten years and a decanter.
records.story: The hill takes its name from a legend: in 1224, the story goes, the knight Gaspard de Stérimberg came home from the crusade against the Albigensians, was granted the slope by Blanche of Castile (1188 to 1252) and lived out his days there as a hermit, beside the chapel at its summit. By the eighteenth century the wine of the hill was sold across Europe, and Bordeaux merchants blended it into their clarets for colour and body. The house began as a wine business at Tain in 1834 and took its name, Paul Jaboulet Aîné, from the founder's elder son. It came to own the chapel and the vines around it, and named its red Hermitage after it. Through the twentieth century La Chapelle was the Hermitage that drinkers abroad knew by name, and its 1961, with the 1978 beside it, became the measure of what northern Syrah can do with age. After a lean spell in the 1990s the family sold the house in 2006 to the Frey family, and the recovery of La Chapelle dates from that sale. To a sommelier it is the name that first taught many drinkers the taste of the hill.

others.name: Hermitage Le Chevalier de Stérimberg
others.note: The white Hermitage of Marsanne and Roussanne, named for the knight of the legend.

others.name: Crozes-Hermitage Domaine de Thalabert
others.note: The house's estate Crozes-Hermitage, Syrah from the flatter land around the hill.

traps: The chapel names the wine and is a landmark; it is no climat of the hill and no classified vineyard.
La Chapelle is the red; Le Chevalier de Stérimberg is the house's white Hermitage.
Domaine de Thalabert is Crozes-Hermitage, the larger appellation around the hill, not Hermitage itself.

cards.front: Paul Jaboulet Aîné's La Chapelle: what is the chapel, and is it a vineyard?
cards.back: The chapel at the summit of the hill of Hermitage, which the house owns; it names the wine, and no climat is called after it.

cards.front: Name the two reference vintages of Hermitage La Chapelle.

questions.q: A guest asks which climats of the hill give most of Hermitage La Chapelle. What do you answer?
opts: Les Bessards and Le Méal
Côte Blonde and Côte Brune
La Crau and Pignan
Reynard and Sabarotte
questions.exp: La Chapelle is drawn chiefly from Les Bessards, granite at the hill's west end, and Le Méal; the Blonde and the Brune are slopes of Côte-Rôtie, and Reynard and Sabarotte are in Cornas.

questions.q: Hermitage La Chapelle went through a lean spell in the 1990s. What happened to Paul Jaboulet Aîné in 2006?
opts: The family sold it to the Frey family
It merged with M. Chapoutier of Tain
The Tain cooperative took it over
It moved its cellars to Valence
questions.exp: The Jaboulet family sold the house to the Frey family in 2006, and the recovery of La Chapelle dates from that sale; Chapoutier is a separate house of Tain.

wine.name: Hermitage
wine.classification: A cru of the Rhône Valley, above Côtes du Rhône and its Villages
wine.grapes: Syrah alone; the family keeps its Marsanne and Roussanne for the white Hermitage.
wine.sites: Parcels across the hill's climats: Les Bessards on granite in the west, L'Ermite high on the slope, then Péléat, Le Méal and Les Rocoules on stonier, lighter ground further east.
wine.making: Each parcel is picked, fermented and raised apart, in vat and then in oak barrels, few of them new, for well over a year. Only then is the one wine assembled, after every lot has been tasted, and bottled at Mauves.
wine.glass: Blackberry, black olive and violet over smoked meat, cracked pepper and graphite, with a note of iron and thyme; layered rather than loud, with dense, fine tannin and a long, savoury finish.
wine.ageing: Reserved for its first decade, it opens slowly and keeps for thirty years and more in a strong vintage.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for two hours, and pour an old one gently off its sediment; a large Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The appellation of the hill above Tain, on the east bank of the Rhône.
The domaine's village, where the wine is bottled, on the west bank across the river from the hill.

records.table: Rather than bottle each climat, Domaine Jean-Louis Chave blends Les Bessards, L'Ermite, Le Méal and others into a single Hermitage, deciding the blend only after tasting every lot. Black olive, pepper and smoked meat, it needs a decade and a decanter.
records.story: By the family's own account its growers can be traced to 1481, and the vines have passed from father to son ever since. They worked the granite terraces of the west bank around Mauves, in what became the Saint-Joseph appellation, and came to hold parcels across the river on the hill of Hermitage. When the Hermitage appellation was drawn in 1937, the hill was already known by its climats, each with its own ground, from the granite of Les Bessards in the west to the lighter, stonier soils further east. Where some houses of the hill came to bottle their climats one by one, the Chaves held to the older idea of Hermitage as a blend of the whole slope, each parcel adding a voice: Bessards the frame, the eastern ground the perfume. The family also makes a white Hermitage that can outlast the red, a rare vin de paille of grapes dried on straw and, in chosen years, Cuvée Cathelin, a selection of the red. Late in the twentieth century it replanted abandoned Saint-Joseph terraces above Mauves. For a sommelier Chave's Hermitage is the case for blending a hill rather than dividing it.

others.name: Hermitage Blanc
others.note: Marsanne with a little Roussanne from the hill, a white that can outlast the red.

others.name: Hermitage Cuvée Cathelin
others.note: A selection of the red made only in chosen vintages, never every year.

others.name: Saint-Joseph
others.note: Syrah from the family's terraces at Mauves and Tournon, across the river from the hill.

traps: Chave blends its climats into one Hermitage; Chapoutier bottles many of its climats separately.
J.L. Chave Sélection is the family's merchant label, not the domaine's own wine.
Cuvée Cathelin is not made every year, so the domaine's Hermitage is the wine of record.

cards.front: Domaine Jean-Louis Chave: how is its red Hermitage put together?
cards.back: Each climat is fermented and raised apart, then blended into one wine after every lot has been tasted.

cards.front: Which rare sweet Hermitage does Domaine Jean-Louis Chave make?
cards.back: A vin de paille, from white grapes dried on straw before pressing.

questions.q: A guest asks why Chave makes one red Hermitage rather than a wine from each climat. Which answer fits?
opts: Each climat adds a part to one wine
The law forbids climat names on Hermitage labels
Its vines lie in Les Bessards alone
Its climats are too young to bottle apart
questions.exp: Chave treats the climats as parts of one wine, Bessards granite for the frame and the eastern ground for perfume; climat names may appear on labels, as Chapoutier's show.

questions.q: By its own account, from which year has the Chave family grown vines in the northern Rhône?
questions.exp: The family dates its line to 1481; 1834 is Jaboulet's founding, 1937 the year of the Hermitage appellation, and 1946 Guigal's founding.

wine.name: Cornas
wine.classification: A cru of the Rhône Valley, above Côtes du Rhône and its Villages
wine.grapes: Syrah alone, as the appellation requires: Cornas admits no white grape at all.
wine.sites: Old vines on steep granite terraces above the village, chiefly Reynard, La Côte, Patou and Sabarotte, blended into this one wine; younger vines go to Renaissance.
wine.making: The bunches go into vat whole, stems and all, and ferment slowly. The wine is then raised for well over a year in large old oak foudres, with no new oak at all, and bottled at the domaine.
wine.glass: Blackberry, tar and black olive over smoked bacon, violet and iron; dark, rugged and tannic in youth, turning with age to smoke, leather and dried thyme.
wine.ageing: Hard and closed for its first eight to ten years, it then softens and keeps for twenty years and more.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for two hours or more, an old one gently; a large glass with room for the aromas.

label.means: The appellation facing Valence across the river, red only and Syrah only, on granite.
The legal guarantee that the wine was grown and made under the rules of Cornas.

records.table: Syrah in its old, unpolished form is what Domaine Auguste Clape bottles as Cornas: whole bunches from granite terraces above the village, raised in big old foudres without new oak. Black olive, tar and smoke when young, it needs years in bottle and an unhurried decanting.
records.story: Cornas faces Valence across the Rhône, and its name, it is said, comes from a Celtic word for burnt earth, for the sun on its granite terraces. The appellation was drawn in 1938, for red wine alone and Syrah alone. For decades most of the village's wine went in bulk to merchants, and the steep slopes, worked by hand, lost their growers to the fruit orchards of the plain. The grower whose name the domaine carries came to Cornas after the Second World War and began to bottle his own wine when few in the village did. He held to the old ways: whole bunches, no new wood, long months in big casks and vines tied to single stakes. His bottles found buyers abroad, and Clape became the address visitors sought when Cornas was barely known beyond the valley. He died in 2018, and his family has kept to the same methods, adding Renaissance from younger vines. For a sommelier Clape's Cornas is the reference for traditional northern Syrah, the wine against which the destemmed, new oak Cornas of later growers is measured.

others.name: Cornas Renaissance
others.note: From the domaine's younger vines: a different bottling, not a selection above the estate Cornas.

others.name: Saint-Péray
others.note: White from Marsanne and Roussanne, from the neighbouring appellation that makes no red.

others.name: Côtes du Rhône
others.note: Syrah from around Cornas sold under the regional name.

traps: Cornas is Syrah only and admits no white grape, unlike Côte-Rôtie, which allows Viognier.
Renaissance is the younger vine Cornas, not a reserve above the estate wine.
Auguste Clape of Cornas has nothing to do with La Clape, the limestone massif of the Languedoc.

cards.front: What may grow beside Syrah in a Cornas, and when was the appellation drawn?

questions.q: A guest compares a young Clape Cornas with a polished, new oak Cornas from another grower. What sets the Clape apart in the cellar?
opts: Whole bunches and large old foudres
Destemmed fruit and new barrels
Co-fermented Viognier for perfume
Carbonic maceration in sealed vats
questions.exp: Clape ferments whole bunches and raises the wine in big old foudres with no new oak; Cornas allows no Viognier, and carbonic maceration is the method of Beaujolais.

questions.q: Before growers such as the founder of Domaine Auguste Clape bottled their own, how was most Cornas sold?
opts: In bulk to merchants
As white wine to Saint-Péray
As Hermitage, across the river
Only to the village's own cafés
questions.exp: For decades most Cornas went in bulk to merchants, so a grower's own bottling gave the village a name abroad; Cornas has always been red, and selling it as Hermitage was never lawful.

wine.name: Condrieu Coteau de Vernon
wine.classification: A cru of the Rhône Valley, above Côtes du Rhône and its Villages
wine.grapes: Viognier alone, as the appellation requires.
wine.sites: Coteau de Vernon, a steep hillside of granite above the town of Condrieu, worked in narrow terraces held up by dry stone walls, where the domaine's old Viognier vines grow.
wine.making: Fermented in oak barrels, few of them new, and raised in them on the lees for well over a year, longer than most Condrieu is kept, before it is bottled at the domaine.
wine.glass: Apricot skin, white peach and honeysuckle over violet, white pepper and wet granite; full and silky, yet held in line by a stony, faintly bitter finish rather than any sweetness.
wine.ageing: Pleasing young, it gains honey, dried apricot and a waxy depth over eight to ten years, which few Condrieu do.
wine.serve: 11 to 13 degrees Celsius, cool rather than cold; no need to decant, though air helps a young bottle; a white Burgundy glass.

label.means: The appellation of Viognier alone on the granite of the northern Rhône, dry unless the label says otherwise.
A lieu-dit, the hillside above the town, not an appellation of its own.

records.table: Coteau de Vernon is Domaine Georges Vernay's Condrieu from old Viognier on a granite hillside above the town, raised in barrel longer than most. Dry, with apricot and violet and a stony, slightly bitter finish, it is a Condrieu to keep rather than drink at once.
records.story: Condrieu's Viognier was once as often sweet as dry, and its steep granite terraces were hard to work and badly paid. The appellation was drawn in 1940, beside the single estate of Château-Grillet, which had been given an appellation of its own in 1936, but after the war the terraces emptied, and by the 1960s only a few growers tended the grape. The grower whose name the domaine carries took over his family's vines in that lean time and refused to let them go: he rebuilt fallen walls, replanted abandoned terraces and, as a leader of the local growers for many years, argued for a dry Condrieu that tasted of its place. When Viognier came into fashion in the 1980s and was planted from California to the Languedoc, his work was a large part of the reason there was a Condrieu left to rediscover. Coteau de Vernon, the old vines on the hill above the town, became the domaine's flagship, made to age rather than to drink at once. His daughter took charge in 1997, and he died in 2017. For a sommelier the wine answers the guest who says Condrieu cannot age.

others.name: Condrieu Les Chaillées de l'Enfer
others.note: From steep, south facing terraces of the appellation, bottled apart.

others.name: Condrieu Les Terrasses de l'Empire
others.note: The domaine's Condrieu for drinking young.

others.name: Côte-Rôtie Maison Rouge
others.note: The domaine's red, Syrah from the slope just north of Condrieu.

traps: Condrieu is dry unless the label says otherwise: Viognier's perfume reads sweet and misleads candidates.
Coteau de Vernon is a lieu-dit within Condrieu, not an appellation of its own; Château-Grillet is the single estate that has one.

cards.front: Domaine Georges Vernay's Coteau de Vernon: which grape, and what is the name on the label?
cards.back: Viognier alone; Coteau de Vernon is a lieu-dit, the granite hillside above the town of Condrieu.

cards.front: Why is the name Vernay tied to the survival of Condrieu?
cards.back: When the appellation shrank to a few growers in the 1960s, the grower behind the domaine kept and replanted its terraces and led its growers.

questions.q: A guest tastes Coteau de Vernon, finds apricot and honeysuckle, and asks if it is sweet. What do you tell them?
opts: It is dry: Viognier's perfume reads as sweetness
It is a late picked sweet Condrieu
It is dry but sweetened before bottling
It is a sweet white from Château-Grillet
questions.exp: Coteau de Vernon is a dry Condrieu, and the apricot perfume of Viognier often reads as sweetness; sweet Condrieu exists but says so on its label.

questions.q: By the 1960s Condrieu had shrunk to a handful of growers. What did the grower behind Domaine Georges Vernay do?
opts: Rebuilt and replanted the abandoned terraces
Replanted the slopes with Syrah for Côte-Rôtie
Sold his vines to the Château-Grillet estate
Moved Viognier down to the flat land by the river
questions.exp: He kept the old terraces, rebuilt their walls, replanted Viognier and led the growers; the slopes stayed Condrieu, and Château-Grillet is a separate single estate.
